en: The Sūtra on Not Guarding the Mind, spoken by the Buddha and translated by the Wu-period Yuezhi upāsaka Zhi Qian.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. The Buddha...
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus replied:
"I have heard that one who guards themselves does not guard themselves.
The bhikṣu then joined his palms and listened to the Buddha.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣu:
"By how many causes and conditions does one fail to maintain self-restraint?

If the faculty of the eye is not closed and guarded, and if the mind flows out toward forms perceived by the eye, then once the mind has flowed out, there is further suffering; because of this further suffering, one cannot attain concentration of mind; because one cannot attain concentration of mind, one does not know reality as it is; and because one does not know reality as it is, one does not see reality as it is. Because one does not know and does not see reality as it is, one neither abandons the fetters nor crosses beyond doubt. Because one neither abandons the fetters nor crosses beyond doubt, one becomes subject to external conditions; being led by what is known as 'other,' one suffers and lacks peace and security."
It is said that it is the same for the ear, the nose, the mouth, the body, and the mind; practicing in this manner is called "not guarding oneself."
The Buddha again addressed the bhikṣus: “By how many causes and conditions does one guard oneself?

If one guards the faculty of the eye, one restrains the visual consciousness so that it does not fall into attachment to forms; when the mind does not stray, one experiences joy (*prīti*); having experienced joy, one attains concentration of mind (*samādhi*); having attained concentration of mind, one realizes the truths (*satya*). Thus, there is knowledge as it truly is and vision as it truly is. Having realized the truths through such knowledge and vision, one abandons the fetters (*saṃyojana*) and transcends doubt. One no longer lacks faith or sincerity, but possesses wisdom and insight, and the mind becomes joyful and at peace. This is said for each of the six faculties in the same way; this is called ‘guarding oneself.’”
"What has been taught regarding self-restraint and lack of self-restraint is thus.
When the Buddha had spoken thus,
they all received it with joy.
The Sūtra on Not Guarding One’s Own Mind Spoken by the Buddha
